title: Travel Protection Plans: Evidence Standard for a Declared Supplier Return
content:
The amount a supplier has paid the traveller is taken, when a restoration is rated against a Travel Protection Plans certificate, at a share which the evidence standing behind it carries. Two records decide that share: whether the supplier's return was raised on the supplier's own disruption, read from the traveller's air booking sold under the Air Ticket Fare Brands and the disruption lines the airline has posted to it, and whether the certificate's claim record names the evidence that supports the claim.

Where the supplier's return was raised on the supplier's own disruption and the certificate's claim record names the evidence that supports the claim, the share which the evidence standing behind it carries is the whole of it, 100 per cent.

Where the supplier's return was raised on the supplier's own disruption and the certificate's claim record names no evidence, the share which the evidence standing behind it carries is 90 per cent.

Where neither holds, the share which the evidence standing behind it carries is 70 per cent.

## The graded share

| The supplier's return raised on the supplier's own disruption | The certificate's claim record | Share the evidence carries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yes | Names the evidence that supports the claim | 100 per cent |
| Yes | Names no evidence | 90 per cent |
| No | Either way | 70 per cent |

## Cases

A case at the whole share: the airline's return stands raised on its own disruption, and the claim filed on the certificate carries a reference for the evidence the traveller supplied. The share is 100 per cent, and the amount the supplier paid is carried into the calculation undiminished by this share.

A case at the middle share: the airline's return stands raised on its own disruption, but the claim filed on the certificate names no evidence at all. The share is 90 per cent.

A case at the lowest share: no return of the airline's stands raised on its own disruption. The share is 70 per cent, and it makes no difference whether the claim record names evidence or not, because both of the higher cases require the return to have been raised on the supplier's own disruption before the claim record is looked at.
